card: Paper card. Question: How does the capacity for twinning-controlled deformation in the equiatomic CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy generate a simultaneous increase in strength and ductility, and what is the origin of its exceptional fracture toughness?. System: Nominally equiatomic CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy (MEA) with a single-phase face-centered cubic (fcc) structure. Processing: Samples extracted from a previously produced alloy; micro-pillars (~300 nm diameter) machined using focused-ion beam (FIB) techniques; in situ TEM compression tests performed at 300 kV; in situ TEM tensile tests conducted at room temperature using a Gatan model 654 single-tilt straining holder at 200 kV; DFT calculations performed using VASP with the nudged-elastic band method. Test conditions: Room temperature (300 K); uniaxial tension and compression; micro-pillar compression at 300 kV; in situ straining at 10 frames per second; DFT calculations at 0 K and 500 K. Findings: The alloy exhibits high strength (~1 GPa), ductility (~60% uniform elongation), and exceptional fracture toughness (KIc > 200 MPa√m).; Ab initio calculations reveal a negative intrinsic stacking-fault energy (γisf = −23 mJ m−2) at 0 K and a high twinnability value (τta = 1.07 ± 0.02).; Deformation activates three twinning systems within individual coarse grains (5–50 μm), forming a stable 3D hierarchical twin network with twin thicknesses ranging from ~100 nm to several micrometres.; Micro-pillars containing a pre-existing {111} twin boundary showed a maximum strength exceeding 2.5 GPa, approximately 1 GPa higher than pillars without a twin.; Dislocations pile up at coherent twin boundaries (CTBs), acting as strong barriers to motion, while intersecting twin boundaries serve as fast channels for dislocation glide.; Dislocations cross-slip between intersecting twin boundaries via an 'overpass' mechanism, enabling homogeneous plastic deformation in three dimensions.; The 3D twin architecture remains stable during deformation with no evidence of twin growth or de-twinning, even as dislocations move rapidly along the boundaries.. Mechanism: The 3D hierarchical twin network provides a dual function: conventional strengthening occurs via the blockage of dislocations impinging on twin boundaries, while the interconnected network offers pathways for dislocation glide along and cross-slip between intersecting twin-matrix interfaces, allowing simultaneous high strength and ductility.. Limitations: The study notes that nano-pillar tests investigate limited volumes; detailed processes of sessile dislocation involvement in cross-slip were not fully captured due to limited time-resolution of in situ TEM; the specific role of magnetization was analyzed but calculations were mainly performed on non-magnetic structures.. Future work: The authors propose that documenting this enhanced twinning-induced toughness may present new directions for the future design of metallic alloys with unprecedented combinations of mechanical properties.. Quote: "This serves a dual function: conventional twin-boundary (TB) strengthening from blockage of dislocations impinging on TBs, coupled with the 3D twin network which offers pathways for dislocation glide along, and cross-slip between, intersecting TB-matrix interfaces."

W2090244344.title: Temperature dependence of the mechanical properties of equiatomic solid solution alloys with face-centered cubic crystal structures

card: Paper card. Question: How do the strength, ductility, and fracture toughness of an equiatomic CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy compare to high-entropy alloys and conventional materials, particularly at cryogenic temperatures, and what mechanisms drive these properties?. System: Equiatomic CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy (MEA). Processing: Arc-melted high-purity elements (>99.9%) under argon, drop-cast into copper moulds, homogenized at 1,200 °C for 24 h, cold-forged and cross-rolled to ~10 mm thickness (60% reduction), then annealed at 800 °C for 1 h in air to achieve a recrystallized microstructure with 5–50 μm grains.. Test conditions: Uniaxial tensile tests at 293 K, 198 K, and 77 K with a strain rate of 10⁻³ s⁻¹; Compact-tension (C(T)) fracture toughness tests at 293 K, 198 K, and 77 K with fatigue pre-cracking and side-grooving per ASTM E1820.. Findings: At 77 K, yield strength reached 657 MPa and ultimate tensile strength reached 1,311 MPa, representing a ~50% increase from room temperature.; Tensile ductility (failure strain) increased to ~0.9 (90%) at 77 K, a ~25% increase from room temperature.; Fracture toughness (KJIc) at crack initiation increased from 208 MPa m1/2 at 293 K to 273 MPa m1/2 at 77 K.; Crack-growth toughness at 77 K reached critical stress-intensity values of ~430 MPa m1/2 (J ~900 kJ m⁻²).; The alloy exhibited a high strain-hardening exponent (n) of 0.4 at cryogenic temperatures.; The CrCoNi alloy showed ~15% higher tensile strength, ~30% higher ductility, and ~50% higher work of fracture than the five-component CrMnFeCoNi alloy at room temperature.; At 77 K, the CrCoNi alloy displayed ~25% higher KJIc, ~27% higher ductility, and ~31% higher work of fracture compared to the CrMnFeCoNi alloy.. Mechanism: The exceptional damage tolerance results from continuous steady strain hardening that suppresses plastic instability, driven by pronounced dislocation activity and deformation-induced nano-twinning. Nano-twinning acts as a dominant deformation mode that provides a steady source of strain hardening, delaying necking and accommodating strain, with its intensity increasing as temperature decreases from room temperature to 77 K.. Limitations: The yield strength at 77 K was slightly lower than the CrMnFeCoNi alloy, attributed to the non-uniform grain size of the current material; the volume fraction of void-initiating inclusions was not accurately quantified relative to the five-component alloy.. Future work: Further studies are needed to accurately determine the relative volume fractions of void-initiating inclusions in the MEA and HEA and to identify their chemistry and crystal structure by TEM after extraction from the voids.. card: Paper card. Question: How can the strength of twinning-induced plasticity (TWIP) steel be enhanced without sacrificing ductility, thereby evading the long-standing strength–ductility trade-off dilemma?. System: FeMnC TWIP steel (23.84% Mn, 0.61% C, balanced Fe) with a low stacking fault energy of 15–30 m Jm−2. Processing: Cylindrical samples were subjected to torsion (180° or 360°) at an angular loading rate of 0.05° s−1 to generate a gradient nanotwinned structure, followed by uniaxial tensile deformation at a strain rate of ~10−4 s−1. Test conditions: Torsion tests at 0.05° s−1; tensile tests at ~10−4 s−1; micro-hardness measured with 500 g load for 15 s; microstructure analyzed via SEM, EBSD, and TEM (200 kV). Findings: Yielding strength of the pre-torsioned TWIP steel was doubled to ~730 MPa (from ~300 MPa) with no reduction in ductility.; A gradient nanotwinned structure formed with twin density increasing from the center to the outermost region (r/R=1).; Twin thickness increased with radial distance, reaching tens of nanometers at the surface.; Subsequent tensile deformation activated secondary and tertiary twins, creating a hierarchical nanotwinned structure.; The hardening modulus remained high until sample failure, unlike traditional processing which reduces ductility.; Finite element simulations showed yielding strength follows a law of mixture, with the hard shell significantly raising the yield strength of the soft core.; Different twinning systems were activated during torsion (e.g., T2, T4) compared to subsequent tension (e.g., T5, T1).; Dislocation dissociation at twin boundaries avoided stress concentration, playing a crucial role in retaining ductility.. Mechanism: The gradient hierarchical nanotwinned structure enhances strength through the hard shell/soft core effect and twin barriers, while ductility is retained because sequential torsion and tension activate different twinning systems, creating a 3D hierarchical network that distributes plasticity and prevents premature failure via localized necking.. Limitations: The method relies on materials prone to deformation twinning (low stacking fault energy); applying the same pre-torsion to 6061 Aluminum alloy resulted in enhanced strength but reduced ductility due to the lack of a hierarchical nanotwin network.. Future work: Develop other methods to produce non-uniform shear strains in metals prone to deformation twinning to enhance material performance, potentially applicable to axially symmetric structural components like axles in machines and high-speed trains.. Quote: "we find that the yielding strength of the material can be doubled at no reduction in ductility."

card: Paper card. Question: What are the atomistic to micro-scale mechanisms underlying the exceptional damage tolerance (high strength, ductility, and fracture toughness) of the single-phase CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy?. System: CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (single-phase fcc solid solution). Processing: Arc-melting high-purity elemental starting materials, drop casting into copper moulds, cold forging and cross rolling at room temperature, recrystallization at 800 °C (grain size ∼6 μm), followed by ion milling (5 kV) or twin jet polishing (10 °C, 13 mA/12 V) to create electron-transparent foils with cracks. Test conditions: In situ straining in an aberration-corrected TEM (FEI Tecnai G2 F20, 200 kV) at room temperature using pulsed tensile loading (axial displacement rate ∼1.0 μm s⁻¹). Findings: Early deformation is dominated by the easy motion of Shockley partial dislocations (1/6<112> type) and the continuous nucleation/annihilation of stacking faults (SFs).; Interactions between partials on different {111} planes form stable 'stacking-fault parallelepipeds' (volume defects) that act as formidable obstacles for dislocation motion.; Perfect (undissociated, 1/2<110> type) dislocations move with extreme difficulty in localized bands of planar slip, creating strong barriers that arrest fast-moving partial dislocations.; The motion of perfect dislocations requires overcoming continuous activation barriers, indicative of high friction stress in the alloy.; Nanoscale voids form in the 'semi-cohesive zone' at the intersection of two {111} slip planes, creating fiber-like bridges spanning the crack faces.; These nanobridges (size <200 nm, some ∼100 nm) deform primarily via nano-twinning ({111} twin structure), which accommodates strain and shields the crack tip.; The synergy of these mechanisms yields tensile strength ∼1 GPa, ductility ∼60–70%, and fracture toughness K_JIc > 200 MPa√m.. Mechanism: The authors propose a synergistic sequence where intrinsic toughening arises from easy partial dislocation motion (ductility) followed by strain hardening via stacking-fault parallelepipeds and planar slip bands (strength). Extrinsic toughening occurs via nanoscale twinned bridges that form behind the crack tip, carrying load and shielding the crack tip from the applied driving force.. Limitations: The study notes that 'ultrahigh-resolution observations have to be made at the nanoscale to permit any characterization of mechanisms so close to the crack tip,' and that 'thin foil samples must be used which, under load, cannot display the full constraint of a bulk sample.'. Future work: The authors state that 'further optimization of these mechanisms may present new directions for the future design of advanced metallic materials with unprecedented damage tolerance.'. Quote: "We identify a synergy of multiple deformation mechanisms, rarely achieved in metallic alloys, which generates high strength, work hardening and ductility"

card: Paper card. Question: How can room-temperature deformation twinning be induced in a high-entropy alloy to improve cryogenic tensile properties, and can non-recrystallized grains be utilized to achieve ultra-high yield strength while maintaining ductility?. System: 10V15Cr5Mn35Fe10Co25Ni (at.%) high-entropy alloy. Processing: Vacuum induction melting followed by homogenization at 1,100 °C for 6 h; cold rolling at room temperature with a 75% reduction ratio to produce 1.5-mm-thick sheets; annealing at 750 °C for 10 min to obtain partially recrystallized microstructure (H750) or at 900 °C for 10 min for fully recrystallized microstructure (H900); water quenching.. Test conditions: Tensile testing at room temperature and cryogenic temperature (−196 °C) using a crosshead speed of 6.4 × 10−3 mm s−1.. Findings: The H750 alloy achieved a yield strength of 970 MPa and a tensile strength of 1,314 MPa at cryogenic temperatures.; The H750 alloy maintained a persistent elongation of 46.3% at cryogenic temperatures.; Non-recrystallized grains in the H750 alloy had an average size of ~32 μm, while recrystallized grains averaged ~1.5 μm.; Deformation twins with thicknesses of 10–30 nm were observed in recrystallized grains at cryogenic temperatures.; Primary twin bundles of ~500 nm thickness and secondary twins of 30–70 nm thickness formed in non-recrystallized grains at cryogenic temperatures.; The yield strength of the H750 alloy was ~270 MPa higher than that of the fully recrystallized H900 alloy at cryogenic temperatures.; Room-temperature cold rolling induced deformation twins in coarse grains without prior hot rolling, which were retained after partial recrystallization.. Mechanism: The critical stress for twinning decreases with increasing grain size, allowing twins to form readily in coarse non-recrystallized grains during cold rolling at room temperature. These retained twins act as strong barriers against mobile dislocations, enhancing yield strength. At cryogenic temperatures, additional deformation twins form in both recrystallized and non-recrystallized regions, leading to a high strain-hardening effect and ultra-high strength.. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study, though it notes that non-recrystallized regions are generally avoided in conventional alloys due to deleterious effects on ductility.. Future work: The authors propose that the combination of room-temperature deformation twinning and non-recrystallization offers a strengthening mechanism for ultra-high-strength HEAs and suggest the alloy is promising for applications in ultra-high-strength HEAs at cryogenic temperatures.. Quote: "Our results demonstrate that non-recrystallized grains, which are generally avoided in conventional alloys because of their deleterious effect on ductility, can be useful in achieving high-strength high-entropy alloys."

card: Paper card. Question: How can a Co-Cr-Ni-based medium-entropy alloy be designed to achieve simultaneous ultra-high strength and sufficient uniform ductility by controlling composition, thermomechanical processing, and microstructural features?. System: Co34.46Cr32.12Ni27.42Al3Ti3 (in at%) medium-entropy alloy with FCC matrix and L12 precipitates. Processing: Vacuum induction melting, homogenization at 1200 °C for 2 h, hot-rolling at 1100 °C (50% reduction), cryo-rolling (CR) at 77 K to 80% total reduction, high-temperature annealing at 900 °C for 1 h (CRA), and subsequent aging at 700 °C for 4 h (CRAA). Test conditions: Uniaxial tensile testing at ambient temperature with a constant strain rate of 1 × 10−3 s−1. Findings: Achieved ultimate tensile strength (σu) of 2.2 GPa and uniform elongation (εue) of 13% in the CRAA-treated alloy.; The dual heterogeneous structure consists of a matrix with coarse grains (10–30 μm) and ultra-fine grains (0.5–2 μm).; Heterogeneous L12 nanoprecipitates range from several to hundreds of nanometers with a total volume fraction of 24.2%.; The lattice mismatch between the FCC matrix and L12 precipitates is extremely low at 0.011%.; The average size of fine L12 precipitates is 4.14 ± 0.62 nm with a number density of 3.4 × 1024 m−3.; Strengthening contributions calculated as: solid-solution (49 MPa), HDI hardening (800 MPa), and precipitation hardening (1115 MPa).; No twins or hexagonal close-packed (HCP) phase formed after deformation up to ~2.0 GPa stress.; Dislocation density in the fractured sample reached 3.83 × 1014 m−2 due to Lomer–Cottrell locks.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the superior properties to a combination of HDI strengthening from the heterogeneous grain structure, precipitation hardening from high-density coherent L12 particles, and enhanced ductility from the low elastic misfit strain of the interfaces which relieves stress concentration and prevents premature fracture, while the preservation of stacking faults and high dislocation density provides significant work-hardening.. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study.. Future work: The authors state that the strategy opens a new avenue for the development of promising heavy-duty structural materials and that the alloy elements and treatments can be readily accepted by industry.. Quote: "a Co-Cr-Ni-based medium-entropy alloy (MEA) with a dual heterogeneous structure of both matrix and precipitates can be designed to provide an ultra-high tensile strength of 2.2 GPa and uniform elongation of 13%"

card: Paper card. Question: How can high-entropy alloys be designed to achieve ultra-high strength while retaining good ductility, overcoming the limitation of near-equiatomic compositions that restrict the formation of high-volume fractions of ductile strengthening precipitates?. System: Al0.5Cr0.9FeNi2.5V0.2 (non-equiatomic, ~50 at% Ni, ~18 at% Cr, ~4 at% V). Processing: Arc-melting pure metals, casting into copper mold, solution-treating at 1200 °C for 24 h followed by water quenching, cold-rolling with 72% reduction ratio, and ageing at 600 °C or 700 °C for 1 h followed by air cooling.. Test conditions: Room temperature tensile testing with a nominal strain rate of 1 × 10−3 s−1 on dog-bone-shaped samples (gauge length 10 mm, width 3 mm, thickness 1 mm).. Findings: Achieved an ultrahigh yield strength of 1810 MPa and ultimate tensile strength of 1905 MPa in the sample aged at 600 °C.; The strength increment relative to the solution-treated sample was >1500 MPa (>560%).; Retained good ductility with elongation of ~9–10% after achieving the maximum strength.; Formed high-content ordered L12 nanoprecipitates with a volume fraction of ~50.1% in the 600 A sample.; The L12 phases are coherent with the FCC matrix, with a lattice parameter difference of only 0.0001 nm (0.3582 nm vs 0.3583 nm).; The spinodal nanostructure contributed 1158 MPa to the yield strength, while grain boundaries contributed 212 MPa.; The total estimated yield strength increase (1524 MPa) agrees closely with the experimental result (1536 MPa).; The mean diameter of the ordered L12 precipitates was determined to be ~35 nm.. Mechanism: The alloying strategy utilizes spinodal decomposition to create a low-misfit coherent nanostructure where the L12 nanophases resist dislocation motion by providing strong diffuse attractive obstacles to trap moving dislocations and by creating antiphase boundaries (APBs) on the slip planes when sheared by dislocations. The diffuse coherent interfaces minimize elastic strain accumulation, preventing crack initiation and maintaining ductility.. Limitations: The authors note that the calculated strengthening contributions based on assuming spherical precipitates may underestimate the area of APBs and the strengthening effect because the actual L12 phases are irregular and interconnected. Additionally, the volume fraction calculations may not be absolutely precise.. Future work: The authors anticipate that this alloying strategy can offer more possibilities for the compositional design of HEAs and will open new avenues for development of ultrastrong and ductile HEAs superior to existing commercial alloys, potentially competing with traditional structural materials in rigorous service conditions.. Quote: "Here we present a strategy to design ultrastrong HEAs with high-content nanoprecipitates by phase separation, which can generate a near-equiatomic matrix in situ while forming strengthening phases"

W2596712240.title: Friction stress and Hall-Petch relationship in CoCrNi equi-atomic medium entropy alloy processed by severe plastic deformation and subsequent annealing

card: Paper card. Question: How can a single-phase face-centered cubic medium-entropy alloy achieve both gigapascal yield strength and high uniform ductility without relying on second-phase heterogeneities?. System: Equimolar CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy (33.48Cr-32.46Co-34.06Ni atomic percent). Processing: Electromagnetic levitation melting, homogenization at 1,473 K for 12 h, hot forging (1,323–1,173 K), cold rolling to 0.5 mm sheets, followed by partial recrystallization annealing at 873 K for 1 h and water quenching. Test conditions: Quasi-static uniaxial tensile tests at strain rate 5 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹, room temperature (298 K) and liquid nitrogen temperature (77 K); loading-unloading-reloading (LUR) tests to measure back stresses. Findings: Yield strength (σ0.2) of ~1,150 MPa achieved with a three-level heterogeneous grain structure (HGS) spanning nanometer to micrometer scales.; Uniform tensile strain (Eu) reached 22% at room temperature, significantly higher than the ~2% Eu observed in homogeneous ultrafine-grained counterparts with similar strength.; The number density of nanograins (ρNG) increased from 4.7 grains/µm² before testing to 21 grains/µm² after deformation at 298 K and 31 grains/µm² at 77 K.; Back stress hardening accounted for over 80% of the total stress elevation observed during strain hardening from yield to ultimate tensile stress.; The strain hardening rate (Θ) exhibited a distinct upturn between 4% and 8% strain, contrasting with the monotonic drop seen in homogeneous structures.; The width of hysteresis loops in LUR tests was the largest ever recorded for any known alloy, indicating exceptionally high internal back stresses.; Corner twins evolved into nanograins during tensile straining, dynamically reinforcing the heterogeneity of the grain structure.. Mechanism: The heterogeneous grain structure induces load partitioning and strain gradient hardening, causing dislocation pile-ups at grain boundaries and generating geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs). This creates large long-range internal back stresses that sustain strain hardening. Additionally, the low stacking fault energy facilitates the dynamic generation of twinned nanograins at grain boundaries during deformation, which further refines the structure and perpetuates back stress hardening.. Limitations: The beneficial effects of the HGS diminish if the material undergoes extended annealing toward uniform grains or if the alloy has high stacking fault energy where full dislocations dominate and recover/annihilate easily.. Future work: The authors propose that this strategy is generally applicable to other single-phase low-SFE alloys and metals to achieve simultaneous high yield strength and high tensile ductility.. Quote: "This heterogeneity results from this alloy's low stacking fault energy, which facilitates corner twins in recrystallization and stores deformation twins and stacking faults during tensile straining."

card: Paper card. Question: Can a hierarchical architecture involving secondary nanoprecipitates form inside primary nanoprecipitates in high-entropy alloys, and can an ultrahigh strength be achieved through a high density of such intragranular hierarchical nanoprecipitates?. System: Fe25Co25Ni25Al10Ti15 (atomic %). Processing: Mechanical alloying (MA) for 49 hours (45h dry + 4h wet with ethanol) followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1000°C, 30 MPa pressure, 90°C/min heating rate, and <8 Pa vacuum.. Test conditions: Room temperature uniaxial tension using in situ SEM microtensile testing with a nominal strain rate of 1 × 10−3 s−1; in situ TEM compression tests at room temperature with an axial displacement rate of 3 nm s–1.. Findings: Tensile yield strength (σ0.2) of ~1.86 GPa and ultimate tensile strength of ~2.52 GPa at room temperature.; Failure strain of ~5.2% achieved alongside the ultrahigh strength values.; Microstructure consists of a primary fcc phase (~82.3 vol %) and a small amount of bcc phase (~17.7 vol %).; The fcc matrix contains a high density of hierarchical intragranular nanoprecipitates: primary γ′ (L12 structure, ~57 nm avg diameter, ~62 vol % in fcc) and secondary γ* (A1 structure, several nm to tens of nm).; Average spacing between adjacent γ′ nanoprecipitates is ~11 nm.; Dislocations were observed to shear both the primary γ′ and secondary γ* precipitates during in situ TEM compression.; Grain diameters average ~409 nm for the fcc phase and ~227 nm for the bcc phase.. Mechanism: The ultrahigh strength is primarily attributed to precipitation strengthening via the shearing mechanism, where dislocations shear both the primary coherent γ′ precipitates and the secondary coherent γ* precipitates, creating an 'exaggerated precipitation strengthening effect' due to the hierarchical obstacle distribution. Additional contributions come from grain-boundary strengthening (due to submicrometer grains) and load transfer via the hard bcc phase.. Limitations: The chemical composition of the secondary γ* precipitates could not be obtained due to their very small sizes.. Future work: The authors suggest the design strategy provides insight for achieving ultrahigh strength in HEAs or other multicomponent alloys, implying further exploration of hierarchical architectures, though specific future experiments are not explicitly detailed beyond the general validation of the strategy.. Quote: "Here, we report a strategy for the design and fabrication of HEAs that can achieve ultrahigh tensile strengths."

card: Paper card. Question: How do additive manufacturing (AM) techniques and post-heat treatments influence the microstructure, mechanical properties, and deformation mechanisms of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) compared to conventional casting methods?. System: CoCrFeNi, AlxCoCrFeNi (x=0.3, 0.6, 0.85), CoCrFeMnNi, FeCoCrAlCu, Ti25Zr50Nb0Ta25, CoCrFeNiTi, and AA5083/CoCrFeNi composites. Processing: Selective Laser Melting (SLM), Laser Metal Deposition (LMD/DMD/DLF), and Selective Electron Beam Melting (SEBM); parameters include layer thickness (20–100 μm), volumetric energy density (VED), laser power (e.g., 400 W), scanning speed (e.g., 1200 mm/s), and pre-heating; post-treatments include High Isostatic Pressing (HIP) at 1100 °C for 2 h, annealing (750–1000 °C), and solution treatment.. Test conditions: Tensile and compression tests at room temperature (298 K) and cryogenic temperature (77 K); microstructural analysis via XRD, SEM, TEM, and EBSD; wear resistance testing.. Findings: AM-processed HEAs exhibit superior yield strength and ductility compared to casting counterparts due to fine microstructures formed by rapid solidification.; SLM CoCrFeNi specimens showed significantly higher yield strength than arc-melt specimens while retaining significant ductility.; Increasing volumetric energy density (VED) in SLM CoCrFeMnNi reduced holes and cracks, leading to higher ultimate tensile strength.; HIP treatment at 1100 °C for 2 h removed second-phase grain-boundary phases and segregation in Al0.3CoCrFeNi, achieving chemical homogenization.; SEBM AlCoCrFeNi specimens displayed better plasticity than cast specimens due to finer grains and a substantial fraction of ductile FCC phase.; Cryogenic testing (77 K) on LAM-fabricated CrMnFeCoNi HEA enhanced yield strength and ductility, with deformation twinning becoming more obvious at high strain.; Solution treatment of SEBM CoCrFeNiTi HEA improved ductility without lowering strength by removing needle-like Ni3Ti precipitates.; Different AM methods induce substantial differences in yield strength and plasticity; for instance, DLF Al0.3CoCrFeNi showed much lower yield strength compared to SLM and SEBM methods.. Mechanism: The enhanced mechanical properties are primarily ascribed to the refinement of microstructures caused by large temperature gradients and rapid solidification during AM, which leads to fine cellular dendrite structures, high dislocation densities, and suppressed elemental segregation. Post-treatments like HIP and annealing further enhance properties by removing fabrication defects (pores, microcracks) and releasing residual stress, while specific heat treatments can dissolve or modify precipitates (e.g., Ni3Ti, B2 phases) to optimize the balance between strength and ductility.. Limitations: Defects such as residual stress, microcracks, and pores exist in as-built AM components, degrading mechanical properties; some AM specimens exhibit anisotropy in mechanical properties due to texture and grain orientation; limited ductility is observed in some Al-rich alloys due to brittle phase appearance; most existing studies focus on tension/compression, with rare data on fracture toughness, fatigue, oxidation, irradiation, or corrosion.. Future work: Optimize processing parameters and heat treatment regimes to improve microstructures and reduce residual stress; investigate fracture toughness, fatigue, oxidation, irradiation, and corrosion properties; expand research to light-weight and refractory HEAs; develop broader compositional ranges; investigate materials with large differences in melting temperatures; and study effective powder blending methods to reduce agglomeration and increase homogeneity.. Quote: "Compared with the casting counterparts, AM-HEAs were found to have a superior yield strength and ductility as a consequence of the fine microstructure formed during the rapid solidification in the fabrication process."

card: Paper card. Question: How do Al and C additions affect the deformation mechanisms (dislocation slip vs. twinning) and strengthening contributions during cold rolling of a CoCrFeNiMn-type high-entropy alloy compared to the equiatomic reference?. System: CoCrFeNiMn-type HEA with composition (20–23) Co, Cr, Fe, Ni; 8.82 Mn; 3.37 Al; 0.69 C (at %). Processing: Self-propagating high-temperature synthesis (SHS) in a centrifugal setup followed by induction remelting in vacuum; cold rolling unidirectionally at room temperature with reductions of 5–10% per pass to final strains of 5%, 10%, 20%, 40%, 60%, and 80%. Test conditions: Room temperature tensile testing at an initial strain rate of 10⁻³ s⁻¹; microhardness testing with 0.3 kg load; microstructural analysis via XRD, EBSD, and TEM. Findings: Initial as-cast alloy had a coarse-grained single fcc structure with grain size of 250–400 μm and yield strength of 210 MPa.; Uniform elongation of the as-cast alloy was 74%, decreasing to 1.3% after 80% cold rolling.; Yield strength increased from 210 MPa (as-cast) to 1310 MPa after 80% rolling reduction.; Dislocation density rose from ~1 × 10¹¹ m⁻² in the as-cast condition to ~2 × 10¹⁵ m⁻² after 40% strain.; Deformation twinning onset was delayed until 20% rolling reduction, whereas the equiatomic reference showed twins after 5%.; Substructure strengthening dominated at rolling reductions <40%, while grain (twin) boundary strengthening prevailed at strains >40%.; The Al-, C-containing alloy exhibited dislocation densities approximately two times higher than the reference CoCrFeNiMn alloy at comparable strains.. Mechanism: The addition of Al and C increases the stacking fault energy (SFE), which suppresses early twinning and promotes planar dislocation slip; this results in higher dislocation density accumulation and a delayed onset of deformation twinning, shifting the dominant strengthening mechanism from substructure hardening at low strains to Hall-Petch (twin boundary) strengthening at high strains.. Limitations: The text notes that exact calculation of the SFE value is a complex problem and could not be fully evaluated due to the absence of other input values for the adapted equation, though the relative difference was confirmed via ∆Ghcp−fcc calculations.. Future work: The authors state that additional studies on the effects of alloying on deformation mechanisms of CoCrFeNiMn-type alloys are required, noting that the effect of Al is even less studied than carbon.. Quote: "The alloy with a chemical composition (at %) of (20–23) Co, Cr, Fe, and Ni; 8.82 Mn; 3.37 Al; and 0.69 C was produced by self-propagating high-temperature synthesis with subsequent induction."

card: Paper card. Question: To determine the influence of Y2O3 nanoparticles on the microstructure, mechanical, and tribological properties of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloys and explore their potential for wear-resistant materials.. System: CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy matrix reinforced with 0, 0.25 wt %, and 0.5 wt % Y2O3 nanoparticles (marked as 0-YOHEA, 0.25-YOHEA, 0.5-YOHEA). Processing: Mechanical alloying of equiatomic elemental powders (Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni) and Y2O3 nanoparticles in a planetary ball mill for 50 h at 300 rpm under Ar atmosphere, followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 900 °C for 5 min under 50 MPa uniaxial pressure in a vacuum of 1 × 10−3 Pa. Test conditions: Room temperature tensile testing (strain rate 1 × 10−3·s−1), Vickers microhardness (1 N load for 15 s), and sliding wear tests (5 N load, 6 mm/s speed, 6 mm distance, 900 s duration, 25 ± 2 °C) against a GCr15 ball (9.525 mm diameter, 766 HV). Findings: The addition of 0.25 wt % Y2O3 increased the room temperature tensile strength from 868 MPa to 1001 MPa (a 15.2% increase) and increased elongation from 5.4% to 6.1%.; The addition of 0.5 wt % Y2O3 resulted in decreased tensile strength and elongation compared to the base alloy and the 0.25 wt % composite.; Microhardness increased from 276 HV (0 wt %) to 403 HV (0.25 wt %) but decreased to 311 HV (0.5 wt %).; The average grain size of the sintered composites decreased with increasing Y2O3 content: 210 ± 50.1 nm (0 wt %), 52 ± 23.2 nm (0.25 wt %), and 31 ± 11.6 nm (0.5 wt %).; The coefficient of friction remained similar across all samples, but the 0.25 wt % Y2O3 composite exhibited the lowest wear loss.; The 0.5 wt % Y2O3 composite showed the highest wear loss and deeper furrows on the worn surface compared to the other samples.; Y2O3 nanoparticles maintained a spherical shape with diameters of approximately 40 nm and 20 nm in the 0.25 wt % and 0.5 wt % composites, respectively.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the strengthening in the 0.25 wt % composite to three mechanisms: grain boundary strengthening (Hall-Petch relation), dispersion strengthening (Orowan looping where dislocations bow around particles), and load transfer from the soft matrix to hard particles. The decrease in properties at 0.5 wt % is attributed to the inverse Hall-Petch effect (softening in nanocrystalline structures) and complicated reasons not fully explained. Wear resistance is attributed to the formation of an oxide layer acting as a solid lubricant and the abrasive nature of Y2O3 particles at higher concentrations.. Limitations: The authors state there is no good explanation for the softening observed in the 0.5 wt % Y2O3 composite despite the fine grain size, noting it may be due to 'complicated reasons'. They also note that the density of the samples showed a decreasing trend compared to theoretical density, though no obvious pores were found in optical images.. Quote: "The addition of 0.25 wt % Y2O3 increased the room temperature tensile strength of the CrMnFeCoNi base from 868 MPa to 1001 MPa"

card: Paper card. Question: How do heat treatments (homogenization and annealing at 900 °C and 950 °C) affect the phase evolution, microstructure, and tensile properties of the Al10Co25Cr8Fe15Ni36Ti6 alloy, and what is the correlation between the γ-γ' morphology, Al-Ni rich needles, and mechanical behavior?. System: Al10Co25Cr8Fe15Ni36Ti6 (at.%) compositionally complex/high entropy alloy. Processing: Vacuum induction melting and directional solidification using the Bridgman method; homogenization at 1220 °C for 20 h; aging at 900 °C for 5 h and 50 h, and at 950 °C for 50, 100, 200, 500, and 1000 h, followed by furnace cooling.. Test conditions: Tensile tests at room temperature and 800 °C with a deformation rate of 0.01 mm/s; Vickers microhardness (~0.5 N load); nanohardness (25 mN load); microstructural analysis via OM, SEM, XRD, and TEM.. Findings: The alloy solidifies dendritically, but the dendritic structure disappears after homogenization at 1220 °C for 20 h.; Annealing at 900 °C or 950 °C leads to the formation of Al-Ni rich needle-like precipitates, with volume fractions increasing from ~1% (900 °C 5 h) to ~13% (950 °C 200 h).; The γ' precipitate size ranges from 6–24 nm after homogenization to 200–550 nm after 900 °C annealing, and up to 400–800 nm after 950 °C annealing.; Tensile strength at room temperature for the 900 °C 50 h state is approximately 1200 MPa, while at 800 °C it is ~580 MPa.; Specimens annealed at 950 °C exhibit widely spread tensile results and brittle fracture due to the high volume fraction of Al-Ni rich needles (~13%).; The 900 °C 50 h annealing produces γ' precipitates with a more defined cuboidal shape (aspect ratio ~0.85–0.9) compared to the 900 °C 5 h state, leading to better mechanical reproducibility.; Nanohardness measurements show the Al-Ni rich needles are harder (>500 HV0.025/20) than the surrounding γ-γ' region (~450 HV0.025/20).; γ' precipitate growth at 950 °C follows the LSW theory of Ostwald ripening (linear growth of radius with t^1/3), whereas growth at 900 °C does not follow this theory.. Mechanism: The authors argue that the high volume fraction of Al-Ni rich needles in the 950 °C annealed states acts as a major factor for early and unpredictable fracture, as the fracture line preferentially follows these needles. In contrast, the 900 °C annealed states benefit from the formation of well-defined cuboidal γ' precipitates which facilitate order hardening and absorb plastic deformation, while the low needle content does not disturb the deformation mechanism.. Limitations: The authors note that the reproducibility of tensile tests is poor for the 950 °C annealed states due to the high abundance of needles, making it almost impossible to determine an average ultimate tensile strength. Additionally, the microhardness values remain constant across states because the indent size (~20 µm) averages over all phases, masking local differences.. Future work: The authors propose to exclude the 950 °C annealing temperature in future studies due to the unwanted needle formation. They expect to improve the ultimate tensile strength at 800 °C by increasing the volume fraction of γ' precipitates through adequate heat treatment or the addition of traces of γ' builders.. Quote: "The amount of needles is a major factor in the fracture behavior of the Al10Co25Cr8Fe15Ni36Ti6 alloy, both concerning the earlier fracture and the reproducibility of the results."
W2889076951.title: Tensile Behavior and Evolution of the Phases in the Al10Co25Cr8Fe15Ni36Ti6 Compositionally Complex/High Entropy Alloy

card: Paper card. Question: What is the fundamental mechanism responsible for the loss of ductility with increasing temperature in single-phase face-centered cubic high-entropy alloys, specifically CrMnFeCoNi?. System: Equiatomic Cr20MnFe20Co20Ni20 (single-phase) and nonequiatomic Cr26Mn20Fe20Co20Ni14 (dual-phase with Cr-rich σ). Processing: Arc melting under argon atmosphere, homogenization at 1200°C for 48 hours, hot rolling at 1100°C to 8 mm, cold rolling to 2.4 mm (70% reduction), annealing at 1000°C for 1 hour (single-phase) or 900°C for 1 hour (dual-phase). Test conditions: Quasi-static tensile tests at 25° to 800°C, strain rate 10⁻³ s⁻¹, samples held at temperature for ~10 min before testing. Findings: Ductility loss in single-phase Cr20MnFe20Co20Ni20 occurs at intermediate temperatures (400° to 700°C) with fracture shortly after ultimate tensile stress.; Fracture mode changes from fully ductile transgranular failure at 25°C to mixed brittle intergranular and ductile transgranular failure at 700°C.; Atom probe tomography reveals nanosized regions (~5 nm thickness) at grain boundaries enriched with Cr, Ni, and Mn after testing at 700°C.; No second-phase precipitates were detected along grain boundaries by XRD, TEM, or SEM-EDS after testing at 700°C.; Cr and Ni segregate separately at grain boundaries, while Ni and Mn tend to cosegregate.; The dual-phase Cr26Mn20Fe20Co20Ni14 alloy exhibits increased ductility with temperature and no intergranular embrittlement at 600° and 700°C.; Trace elements C and B segregate at grain boundaries but at concentrations (0.2 at% C, 0.008 at% B) insufficient to form carbides or borides.. Mechanism: Ductility loss is caused by the fast segregation of principal elements (Cr, Ni, Mn) into grain boundaries during deformation at intermediate temperatures, forming nanoclusters that reduce grain boundary cohesion and promote crack initiation. The authors propose that Cr and Ni segregate separately due to repulsion, while Ni and Mn cosegregate, potentially forming brittle phases or reducing cohesion via magnetic contributions. Preexisting Cr-rich σ phases can absorb these embrittling elements, preventing their segregation to grain boundaries.. Limitations: The study notes that grain refinement in HEAs can assist the segregation of principal elements to grain boundaries and lead to brittle intermetallic phases, making grain refinement ineffective for avoiding this specific embrittlement. Additionally, the dual-phase alloy designed for proof-of-concept has lower ductility than the single-phase alloy below 500°C.. Future work: The authors suggest that the ductility of HEAs at intermediate temperatures can be further improved if the morphology, dimension, and distribution of secondary phases are optimized further following the proposed GB segregation engineering strategy.. Quote: "Nanoclustering Cr, Ni, and Mn separately at GBs, as detected by atom probe tomography, reduces GB cohesion and promotes crack initiation along GBs."

card: Paper card. Question: What are the phase-specific mechanical behaviors, deformation mechanisms, and phase-boundary interactions in the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high entropy alloy under small-scale loading?. System: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high entropy alloy (lamellar arrangement of L12 and B2 solid-solution phases). Processing: Vacuum arc-melting of pure elements (>99.9% purity) with homogenization via multiple flips and re-melting cycles; samples polished to 0.02 µm roughness; micro-pillars prepared via FIB (30 kV Ga+ down to 5 kV) with final diameter 2.0 ± 0.3 µm and aspect ratio ~2; bulk specimens prepared via EDM (tensile) and machining (compression). Test conditions: Bulk tensile/compression at 10^-3 s^-1; nano-indentation at 10000 µN and 500 µN loads; strain rate sensitivity at 4×10^-2, 1.2×10^-1, and 4×10^-1 s^-1; micro-pillar compression at ~2.5×10^-4 s^-1; scratch tests at 500 mN load with ramping to 3000 µN. Findings: Ultimate tensile strength of 1165 ± 20 MPa with ~18% elongation; ultimate compressive strength of 1863 ± 12 MPa with ~34% fracture strain.; B2 phase showed higher hardness (7.5 ± 2.2 GPa at 500 µN) compared to L12 phase (6.0 ± 0.5 GPa).; B2 phase exhibited higher strain rate sensitivity (SRS) than L12, with bulk SRS close to B2 values.; Micro-pillar yield strength was ~610 MPa for B2 and ~460 MPa for L12; mixed pillars showed double yielding at ~350 MPa and ~620-640 MPa.; B2 phase deformed via plastic barreling with limited slip steps, while L12 phase showed high density of slip steps and homogeneous flow.; Coefficient of friction was ~0.89 for B2 and ~0.83 for L12; L12 showed more material pile-up during scratch tests.; Phase boundary remained preserved without separation or cracking even after high compressive strains in mixed micro-pillars.. Mechanism: The B2 phase controls deformation due to its higher strength and SRS, while the L12 phase accommodates plasticity through multiple slip systems. The semi-coherent phase boundary prevents crack propagation and separation, contributing to high strength and ductility. Cr-rich nano-precipitates (~20 nm) in the B2 phase act as barriers to dislocation movement, enhancing strength. The tension-compression asymmetry arises from lamellar orientation, elastic property differences, and volume fractions of the phases.. Limitations: The study notes that multiple yield points were not detected in bulk tests likely due to the small difference in modulus between phases and lower resolution of bulk experiments. The anisotropic behavior may depend on the location of samples due to varying cooling conditions in the ingot.. Future work: The authors state these results will pave the way for fundamental understanding of phase-specific contributions to bulk mechanical response and help in designing structural materials with high fracture toughness.. Quote: "Dual mode fracture was observed with ductile failure for L12 phase and brittle mode for B2 phase."

card: Paper card. Question: How to achieve a simultaneous balance of high fracture strength and high ductility in high-entropy alloys while overcoming inferior castability and compositional segregation?. System: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA). Processing: Vacuum induction melting of commercially pure elements (Al, Co, Ni: 99.9 wt.%; Cr, Fe: 99.5 ~ 99.6 wt.%) in a BN crucible; heating to 600°C for 1 hour; pouring at 1500°C into a MgO crucible (220 mm length, 62 mm upper ID, 50 mm bottom ID) under argon atmosphere (0.06 MPa); bulk ingot weight ~2.5 kg.. Test conditions: Room temperature tensile tests at strain rate 1 × 10−3 s−1; elevated temperature tests at 600°C and 700°C at strain rate 1 × 10−3 s−1; cold rolling with 8% thickness reduction followed by tensile testing at 2 × 10−3 s−1.. Findings: The as-cast alloy exhibited a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure with an inter-lamellar spacing of about 2 μm.; Room temperature tensile test showed a fracture stress of 944 MPa and an elongation of 25.6%.; The proof stress was 75 MPa, while the fracture stress reached close to 1.2 GPa (true stress condition).; At 600°C, the alloy maintained a fracture stress of 806 MPa and elongation of 33.7%.; At 700°C, the alloy maintained a fracture stress of 538 MPa and elongation of 22.9%.; Cold rolling with 8% reduction increased the true fracture stress to 1265 MPa while maintaining 9.9% elongation.; The density of the EHEA was measured to be 7.38 g/cm3.; The ratio of fracture strength to proof stress (σUTS/σ0.2) was close to 16.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the unprecedented strain hardening and balanced properties to the fine regular lamellar structure that easily stores dislocations and the alternating soft fcc phases and hard B2-structured NiAl-rich phases. When dislocations pass through soft fcc phases, the hard B2 phases, including nanoscale precipitates, pin the movement of dislocations resulting in significant work hardening.. Limitations: The text notes that the mechanism for the low elastic limit (proof stress) is still unclear at this stage.. Future work: Further exploration of new EHEAs will be based on physical metallurgy principles using atomic radius, mixing enthalpy, and valence electron concentration; thermodynamics calculations based on the CALPHAD method can provide guidance once reliable databases are established; the potential for producing ultrahigh strength components after large plastic deformation awaits further investigations.. Quote: "To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases."

card: Paper card. Question: How can cryo-rolling and annealing be utilized to overcome the strength-ductility trade-off in multiphase high entropy alloys, specifically regarding the development of a hierarchical microstructure?. System: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high entropy alloy (EHEA). Processing: Multi-pass cryo-rolling up to ~90% reduction in thickness with immersion in liquid N2 for 45 minutes before and after each pass, followed by annealing at 800 °C for 1 hour and water quenching.. Test conditions: Tensile tests at ambient temperature with an initial strain rate of 8.3 × 10−4 s−1; Nano-indentation with load increased linearly from 1 μN to 500 μN over 0.25 seconds.. Findings: The cryo-rolled and annealed material achieved a Yield Strength (YS) of 1437 ± 26 MPa and Ultimate Tensile Strength (UTS) of 1562 ± 33 MPa.; The elongation to failure (ef) was approximately 14 ± 1%, which remained almost unchanged compared to the as-cast material (17 ± 1%).; The hierarchical microstructure consists of fine lamellar regions with ultrafine FCC grains (average size ~200–250 nm) and coarse non-lamellar regions with coarse unrecrystallized B2 phase (~2.5 µm).; The hardness of the B2 phase (~12 GPa) is nearly three times higher than that of the L12 phase (~4 GPa) in the as-cast material.; The cryo-rolled and annealed material covers the entire hardness spectrum with softer regions (≤8 GPa), intermediate regions (~8–12 GPa), and much harder regions (≥12 GPa).; The cold-rolled and annealed material showed a homogenous microduplex morphology with grain sizes of ~0.5 µm, unlike the heterogeneous cryo-rolled structure.; The cryo-rolled and annealed EHEA possesses the highest YS and UTS while maintaining appreciable ductility compared to other HEAs like Al0.5CoCrCuFeNi and Fe40Mn27Ni26Co5Cr2.. card: Paper card. Question: What are the strength and deformation mechanisms of nanocrystalline Al0.3CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy thin films (HEATFs) compared to bulk samples?. System: Al0.3CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy thin films. Processing: Magnetron sputtering deposition on silicon wafer substrates; target cleaned by argon ion bombardment for ~2 min; substrate rotation speed 2 rpm; film thickness ~4 μm; nanopillars (diameter 738 nm) fabricated by FIB at 30 kV/10 pA. Test conditions: Room temperature; nanoindentation with Berkovich tip (depth <10% of film thickness); in situ SEM compression using flat punch diamond tip at strain rate ~5×10-3 s-1. Findings: Surface roughness Ra is less than 5 nm (specifically <3.5 nm in some profiles).; Grain size is approximately 10 nm with a homogeneous chemical composition.; Main phase is face-centered cubic (FCC) with a minor ordered BCC NiAl type phase.; Hardness is approximately 11.09 GPa, which is about three times that of bulk samples.; Elastic modulus is approximately 186.01 GPa, nearly the same as bulk samples.; Yield strength of nanopillars is approximately 1024 MPa, about three times that of bulk samples.; Compressive strength reached ~2075 MPa at a strain of ~11.39% before softening.; Plastic deformation is inhomogeneous and localized, occurring first at the top of the pillar.. Mechanism: The enhanced hardness is ascribed to the nanocrystalline strengthening mechanism induced by a large number of grain boundaries. The inhomogeneous plastic deformation is characterized by localized metal flow and slip generation at the top of the nanopillar.. Limitations: The text notes that a rigorous diffraction-intensity-distribution calculation of the solid solution phases responsible for certain orientations is beyond the scope of this work.. Future work: The results could provide an in-depth understanding of the mechanics and deformation mechanism for future design of nanocrystalline HEATFs with desired properties.. card: Paper card. Question: How can the limited ductility of eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs) be overcome to achieve ultra-ductility while maintaining high strength?. System: Ni30Co30Cr10Fe10Al18W2 (at%) eutectic high-entropy alloy consisting of FCC and B2 phases; industrial A357 casting aluminum alloy. Processing: Two cycles of 30% cold rolling followed by annealing at 1200 °C for 20 mins with water quenching; for A357: two cycles of 15% cold rolling at 540 °C for 40 mins followed by two cycles of 30% cold rolling at 540 °C for 40 mins. Test conditions: Quasi-static uniaxial tensile tests at room temperature with an initial strain rate of 1 × 10−3 s−1; in situ tensile tests in FE-SEM; loading-unloading-reloading tests for back stress measurement. Findings: The phase-selectively recrystallized (PSR) EHEA achieves a uniform elongation of ∼33% and an engineering ultimate tensile strength approaching ∼2.2 GPa.; The PSR EHEA exhibits a fracture true strain of ∼30%, which is double that of the As-cast (AC) alloy (∼14%) and the fully recrystallized (FR) alloy (∼17%).; The fracture true stress of the PSR EHEA reaches ∼1850 MPa, significantly higher than the AC (∼1390 MPa) and FR (∼1460 MPa) alloys.; The microcrack density in the fractured PSR specimen is only one-third of that in the FR specimen, even under a twofold nominal strain.; The local von Mises strain in the FCC phase can be up to 6 times higher than that in the B2 phase during deformation.; A back stress of ∼900 MPa near failure was quantitatively measured in the PSR EHEA, accounting for its high strain hardening capacity.; A B2 → body-centered tetragonal (BCT) phase transformation was observed in the PSR EHEA during deformation, with the crystal structure expanding ∼6% along the (200) direction.; The PSR strategy increased the elongation of the A357 aluminum alloy from ∼8% to ∼23% and doubled its tensile strength to ∼400 MPa.. Mechanism: Phase-selective recrystallization (PSR) eliminates weak boundaries (lamellar phase boundaries in AC and high-density grain boundaries in FR) by inducing complete recrystallization in the soft FCC phase while maintaining a skeletal, non-recrystallized B2 phase that undergoes only recovery. This microstructure prevents premature crack nucleation at weak interfaces, allowing both phases to contribute to strain hardening simultaneously through high-density dislocation multiplication and a strain-induced B2 to BCT phase transformation, thereby exhausting the alloy's strain hardening capacity before fracture.. Limitations: The proposed model for calculating the suitable deformation level for PSR is semi-quantitative because it ignores information on microstructure and strain rate.. Future work: Further modifications to the theoretical model to include microstructure and strain rate information; direct characterization of PSR behaviors under different rolling amounts and subsequent annealing to overcome the complexity of acquiring parameter values.. Quote: "The PSR EHEA with a well-tailored PSR microstructure doubles the fracture strain to ∼30%."

card: Paper card. Question: How can the strength–ductility synergy in eutectic high-entropy alloys be improved by inheriting the composite lamellar nature through tailored thermo-mechanical processing?. System: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (at%) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA). Processing: Arc-melting followed by suction-casting into a copper mold, multi-pass cold-rolling to 84–86% reduction in thickness, and non-isothermal annealing at 660, 700, 740, or 900 °C for 1 h with a heating rate of 10 °C min−1 followed by water quenching.. Test conditions: Room temperature tensile tests with an initial strain rate of 2.5 × 10−4 s−1 using dog-bone specimens (15 mm gauge length, 3.2 mm width, 600 μm thickness) and loading–unloading–reloading (LUR) tests.. Findings: The DPHL700 and DPHL740 samples achieved a yield strength of approximately 1.5 GPa with an elongation of ~16%, representing a simultaneous enhancement in both strength and ductility compared to as-cast and ultrafine-grained counterparts.; The microstructure exhibited a two-hierarchical heterogeneity consisting of submicron-grade FCC/B2 grains within FCC lamellae and micron-grade alternate FCC/B2 lamellae.; The average diameters of FCC and B2 grains were roughly comparable at ~0.71 μm, with inter-lamella spacings ranging from 1.5 to 5 μm.; Phase decomposition resulted in two types of NiAl-rich precipitates in FCC lamellae: small intragranular P1 grains (50–180 nm) and large intergranular P2 grains (~350 nm).; Back-stress measurements at the yield point reached ~950 MPa, which was approximately 3 times higher than the effective stress, primarily responsible for the high yield strength.; The strain-hardening rate (Θ) showed a transient behavior with an up-turn in region II and sustained high Θ over a wide strain region III for DPHL700.; Microcrack-arresting mechanisms were observed where multiple microcracks were inhibited from coalescing, with ductile components acting as efficient crack arresters.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the enhanced properties to a two-hierarchical constraint effect that generates long-range back-stress by storing geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs) due to strain gradients at lamella interfaces and around intergranular precipitates, combined with a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism where the aligned lamellar architecture delays crack propagation and coalescence.. Limitations: The authors note that while the DPHL structure is effective, increasing the annealing temperature to 900 °C induced a partially degraded lamellar structure that led to inferior tensile properties, indicating the sensitivity of the process to thermal treatment.. Future work: The authors propose that further efforts should be devoted to exploring non-equiatomic alloys and spinodal decomposition to create low-misfit coherent nanostructures for even higher yield strengths, and anticipate modifying the EHEA to satisfy requirements for high-temperature and/or corrosion environments.. Quote: "The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism."

card: Paper card. Question: How can fatigue life be enhanced in high-entropy alloys at low strain amplitudes without sacrificing ductility, specifically by addressing the trade-off between fatigue strength and fatigue-crack-initiation resistance in precipitation-strengthened alloys?. System: Al0.5CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy containing an FCC matrix and multicomponent B2 precipitates (NiAl-type). Processing: Vacuum-induction melting to fabricate a large plate, followed by hot rolling with 60% reduction at 1150 °C, and annealing at 1000 °C for 1 h. Test conditions: Monotonic tension at RT with a strain rate of 1 × 10−3 s−1; fully-reversed strain-controlled low-cycle fatigue (LCF) at RT with strain amplitudes from ±0.1% to ±1.75% and a strain rate of 1 × 10−2 s−1; real-time in situ neutron diffraction at strain amplitudes of ±0.5%, ±1%, and ±1.75%. Findings: The alloy exhibits at least four times longer fatigue life than conventional alloys at a plastic strain amplitude of ~0.03%.; The B2 phase bears significantly more stress than the FCC phase after yielding, with lattice strains nearly ten times larger.; Stress-induced martensitic transformation (SIMT) occurs in the B2 phase, evidenced by abnormal peak broadening and peak separation in neutron diffraction.; Deformation twinning is observed in the FCC matrix only at high strain amplitudes (≥1.75%), not at intermediate amplitudes (1%).; The B2 phase is plastically deformable at all tested strain amplitudes, storing dislocations and relieving stress concentration.; Fine B2 precipitates act as efficient crack arresters, forming blunted cracks, whereas coarse band-like B2 precipitates initiate microcracks.; The multicomponent B2 phase has lower antiphase boundary (APB) energies (e.g., compared to 0.697 eV/m² for pure NiAl) enabling plastic deformation.. Mechanism: The enhanced fatigue life is attributed to the ductile-transformable character of the multicomponent B2 precipitates, which undergo reversible martensitic transformation and plastic deformation to accommodate strain incompatibility with the FCC matrix. This mechanism relieves stress concentration at phase boundaries, retards microcrack initiation, and provides alternative deformation pathways, unlike brittle traditional intermetallics.. Limitations: The study notes that if the B2 phase size is too large (e.g., band-like precipitates), it becomes easy to initiate microcracks due to longer incoherent interfaces where stress concentration cannot be effectively accommodated.. Future work: The authors propose that the design strategy of introducing ductile-transformable multicomponent intermetallic precipitates can guide the design of fatigue-resistant alloys by tuning HEA compositions and thermomechanical processing.. Quote: "the current HEA shows at least four times longer life than conventional alloys"

card: Paper card. Question: How does the processing temperature (77 K vs. 300 K) during high-pressure torsion (HPT) affect the microstructure evolution, phase stability, and mechanical properties (hardness and tensile strength) of the Co20Cr26Fe20Mn20Ni14 high-entropy alloy, particularly regarding the phenomenon of natural aging?. System: Co20Cr26Fe20Mn20Ni14 high-entropy alloy (low stacking fault energy of 3.5 mJ/m2). Processing: High-pressure torsion (HPT) at 77 K (cryogenic) and 300 K (room temperature) under 5 GPa pressure for 1, 3, and 5 anvil turns; samples held for natural aging up to two months.. Test conditions: Vickers hardness (300 g load, 10 s dwell) measured at 10 min, 1 day, 2 weeks, 1 month, and 2 months post-processing; tensile testing (strain rate 10^-3 s^-1) conducted 2 weeks post-processing; XRD, SEM, EBSD, and TEM analysis performed.. Findings: Cryogenic HPT resulted in lower mechanical strength (hardness and tensile strength) compared to room temperature HPT after natural aging.; Vickers hardness of cryo-HPT samples dropped precipitously after two weeks of natural aging, whereas room temperature HPT samples showed no hardness decrease over one month.; Deformation-induced FCC-to-HCP phase transformation occurred in the alloy processed by cryo-HPT, confirmed by XRD and TEM.; Dislocation density in cryo-HPT samples was very high (~1.0 to 2.5 × 10^16 m^-2) immediately after processing but decreased significantly with natural aging time.; Room temperature HPT produced an average grain size of 61 ± 25 nm, while cryo-HPT resulted in larger average grain sizes (e.g., 5.42 ± 1.69 μm after 5 turns).; The volume fraction of deformation twins decreased from 48% in the annealed state to 0.6% after 5 turns of cryo-HPT.; The σ phase peaks observed in the annealed state almost disappeared after HPT processing at both 77 K and 300 K.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the lower strength and hardness drop in cryo-HPT samples to 'self-annealing' (static recovery and static recrystallization) during natural aging, driven by the high stored energy from deformation and the low stacking fault energy which inhibits cross-slip and dynamic recrystallization during processing but allows static recovery afterward. The FCC-to-HCP transformation is rationalized as a kinetically possible transition due to high pressure and low temperature overcoming the energy barrier.. Limitations: The authors note that extreme grain refinement during cryo-HPT cannot be entirely ruled out, as nano-grained structures might have been unstable at room temperature and underwent recovery before characterization.. Quote: "Cryogenic HPT was found to result in a lower mechanical strength of alloy Co20Cr26Fe20Mn20Ni14 than room temperature HPT."

card: Paper card. Question: Is polymorphism still possible in entropy-stabilized high-entropy alloys (HEAs) that are generally believed to possess extremely high structural stability and maintain a single-phase structure?. System: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy (Cantor's alloy). Processing: Synthesized via gas-atomization (melt injected into high purity Ar at 4 MPa pressure); subjected to hydrostatic compression up to ~41 GPa using a diamond anvil cell (DAC) with helium as pressure-transmitting medium; subsequently heated using resistive heating (up to 723 K) or double-sided Nd:YLF laser heating (up to ~1,400 K) at various pressures (6, 14, 26 GPa).. Test conditions: Room temperature compression up to ~41 GPa; heating at ambient pressure up to 723 K; heating at 6, 14, and 26 GPa up to ~1,400 K; in situ synchrotron radiation X-ray diffraction (XRD) monitoring.. Findings: The fcc-to-hcp polymorphic transition starts at approximately 22 GPa and almost completes at approximately 41 GPa.; The phase transition is irreversible; the hcp phase is retained when pressure is released to ambient conditions.; The hcp phase remains stable up to 633 K at ambient pressure before transforming back to fcc.; At 26 GPa, the critical temperature for the hcp-to-fcc transition is approximately 1,400 K.; The isothermal bulk modulus (B0) is 153.9±3.0 GPa for the fcc phase and 150.2±4.6 GPa for the hcp phase.; The c/a ratio of the hcp phase remained almost constant at 1.62±0.01 during compression and decompression.; The transition is sluggish, with fcc and hcp phases coexisting over a wide pressure range of ~22 to ~41 GPa.; Decompression from different maximum pressures yields fcc/hcp composites with tunable fractions.. Mechanism: The transition occurs because the hcp structure is thermodynamically more favorable at lower temperatures and high pressures, while the fcc phase is stable at higher temperatures and lower pressures; the transition is kinetically hindered by high energy barriers and low stacking fault energy (~20 mJ m−2), requiring high pressure to overcome these barriers to form the hcp phase.. Limitations: The transition is sluggish and irreversible, making it difficult to determine the real equilibrium phase boundary (Clapeyron coexistence curve) experimentally; grain size was not small enough for statistically reliable Rietveld refinement of volume fractions; overshooting often exists due to high energy barriers.. Future work: The authors suggest that this behavior could be general in various HEAs and propose new avenues for tailoring HEA properties via polymorphic transition-induced HEA composites, particularly at cryogenic temperatures where transition pressure could be largely decreased.. Quote: "The transition is irreversible, and our in situ high-temperature synchrotron radiation X-ray diffraction experiments at different pressures of the retained hcp high-entropy alloy reveal that the fcc phase is a stable polymorph at high temperatures, while the hcp structure is more thermodynamically favourable at lower temperatures."

card: Paper card. Question: How does the composition of refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) based on Ti, Zr, Hf, V, and Nb affect their elastic properties, ideal tensile strength (ITS), and intrinsic ductility?. System: Four body-centered cubic (bcc) refractory HEAs: ZrNbHf, ZrTiNbHf, ZrVTiNb, and ZrVTiNbHf. Processing: Ab initio alloy theory using the exact muffin-tin orbitals (EMTO) method combined with the coherent-potential approximation (CPA) within the local-density-approximation (LDA) exchange-correlation density functional; Brillouin zone integrations on a 27 × 27 × 27 k-points mesh. Test conditions: Uniaxial tension along the [001] direction; quasi-static procedure with relaxation of unit cell lattice vectors perpendicular to [001] to allow symmetry lowering deformation. Findings: The ITS of the ternary ZrNbHf alloy amounts to 2.64 GPa.; Adding equimolar Ti to ZrNbHf decreases the ITS to 2.28 GPa.; Adding both Ti and V to ZrNbHf enhances the ITS by nearly 42% compared to ZrNbHf.; Substituting Hf in ZrNbHf with equiatomic Ti and V increases the ITS by about 170%.; All investigated HEAs possess high elastic anisotropy with Zener anisotropy ratios indicating anisotropic behavior.; All HEAs show good extrinsic ductility with B/G ratios larger than 3.5 and positive Cauchy pressure.; The ZrVTiNb alloy exhibits an intrinsic brittle-to-ductile transition, failing via shear instability rather than cleavage.; The ITS correlates strongly with the fcc-bcc structural energy difference (SED) and average d-band occupation.. Mechanism: The ideal tensile strength is determined by the ratio of group four elements to group five elements, which controls the average d-band filling; higher d-occupation leads to higher structural energy difference (SED) and consequently higher ITS, while specific d-band fillings (around 3.15) induce shear instabilities leading to intrinsic ductility.. Limitations: The study is limited to ab initio predictions of ideal strength for defect-free crystals and does not account for extrinsic factors like dislocations, grain boundaries, or cracks that control strength in real materials.. Future work: The authors suggest that HEAs with d-band fillings larger than ~3.2 are expected to be intrinsically ductile and reach ITS values approaching those of group five elements as d-occupation approaches ~3.6.. Quote: "The ITS of the ternary ZrNbHf alloy amounts to 2.64 GPa, and slightly decreases to 2.28 GPa by adding the fourth element Ti."

card: Paper card. Question: How does post-HPT annealing affect the microstructure evolution and the combination of tensile strength and ductility in CoCrNi medium entropy alloy?. System: CoCrNi medium entropy alloy (single FCC phase). Processing: Vacuum induction melting, homogenization, cold rolling, recrystallization, High-Pressure Torsion (HPT) to achieve ~50 nm grain size, followed by annealing in Ar atmosphere at 600–800 °C for 2–60 min. Test conditions: Vickers hardness (300 gf load, 15 s dwell); uniaxial tensile testing at quasi-static strain rate of 10⁻³ s⁻¹ with digital image correlation; EBSD and TKD characterization. Findings: Samples annealed at 700 °C for 15 min exhibit a tensile strength of ~1090 MPa and strain to failure of ~41%.; Annealing at 600 °C for 60 min and 700 °C for 2 min results in partially recrystallized microstructures with average grain sizes of ~600–670 nm and average KAM values of ~0.83–0.84°.; Samples annealed at 700 °C for 15 min and longer durations show nearly fully recrystallized microstructures with grain sizes ranging from ~960 nm to 5 µm and average KAM values of 0.37°–0.45°.; The fraction of low angle grain boundaries is higher in partially recrystallized samples and decreases significantly with increasing annealing time and temperature.; Samples with partially recrystallized microstructures exhibit strain softening behavior followed by strain hardening, whereas fully recrystallized samples show only strain hardening.; The increase in work hardening rate (WHR) in the softening zone for partially recrystallized samples is attributed to the fraction of low angle grain boundaries.; No sigma phase or secondary phases were observed in the temperature range of 600–800 °C.. Mechanism: Superior mechanical properties are attributed to fine grains, fine annealing twins, high shear stress, high friction stress, and low-angle grain boundaries. Low angle grain boundaries allow defects to pass through rather than pile up, reducing work hardenability and uniform elongation but increasing strain to fracture. The increase in WHR in the softening zone for partially recrystallized samples is linked to the fraction of low angle grain boundaries.. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study.. Future work: The text does not explicitly state future work.. Quote: "The sample annealed at 700 °C for 15 min exhibits a remarkable combination of tensile strength (~1090 MPa) and strain to failure (~41%)."

card: Paper card. Question: How can interstitial carbon be utilized to unify multiple metallic strengthening mechanisms in a high-entropy alloy to achieve simultaneous high strength and ductility?. System: Fe49.5Mn30Co10Cr10C0.5 (at%) interstitial high-entropy alloy (iHEA), specifically a metastable TRIP-assisted dual-phase system with f.c.c. γ matrix and h.c.p. ε phase. Processing: Vacuum induction melting of pure metals and carbon; hot-rolling at 900 °C (50% thickness reduction); homogenization at 1200 °C for 2 h in Ar followed by water-quenching; cold-rolling (60% reduction) and annealing at 900 °C for 3 min in Ar followed by water-quenching. Test conditions: Uniaxial tensile testing at room temperature (293 K) with an engineering strain rate of 1 × 10−3 s−1. Findings: The grain-refined iHEA exhibits tensile strength nearly twice that of a single-phase equiatomic FeMnCoCrNi alloy while maintaining identical elongation.; The grain-refined iHEA shows ~100 MPa (~15%) higher yield and ultimate strength compared to a grain-refined TRIP-DP-HEA.; The fraction of transformed h.c.p. phase at the necking stage (εloc = 90%) is 36.5% (area%), indicating higher f.c.c. phase stability than substitutional TRIP-DP-HEAs (>75%).; Nano-twinning is observed as an essential additive deformation mechanism during early uniform deformation (εloc = 10%), unlike in TRIP-DP-HEAs where it occurs only later.; Nano-particles with an average size of 50~100 nm, identified as M23C6 carbides, are randomly distributed in the matrix with a volume fraction of ~1.5 vol.%.; The alloy unifies eight strengthening mechanisms: massive substitutional solid solution strengthening, interstitial solid solution strengthening, dual-phase composite effect, nano-particle strengthening, TWIP, TRIP, stacking fault formation, and grain size reduction.; The coarse-grained iHEA shows superior mechanical response with higher elongation and identical ultimate strength compared to a coarse-grained TRIP-DP-HEA.. Mechanism: The addition of interstitial carbon increases the stacking fault energy and phase stability of the f.c.c. matrix, triggering a joint activation of twinning-induced plasticity (TWIP) and transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) while maintaining the dual-phase structure. This is combined with massive substitutional and interstitial solid solution strengthening, Orowan strengthening from nano-carbides, and grain boundary strengthening from grain refinement.. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study, though it notes that the true temperature during the short annealing time might be lower than the furnace temperature of 900 °C.. Future work: The authors propose that 'further optimization potential is at hand' due to the 'option for interstitial-driven tuning of phase (in)stability' and suggest that the design concept has 'very large potential to break the inverse strength-ductility relationship.'. Quote: "The new interstitial TWIP-TRIP-HEA thus unifies all metallic strengthening mechanisms in one material, leading to twice the tensile strength compared to a single-phase HEA with similar composition, yet, at identical ductility."

card: Paper card. Question: What are the bulk critical resolved shear stress (CRSS), the size effect scaling exponent, the stacking fault energy, and the magnitude of solid-solution strengthening in the equatomic CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy?. System: Equatomic CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (FCC structure). Processing: Arc-melting of high-purity elements in argon, cold-rolling (60% reduction), recrystallization at 1,173–1,473 K; single-crystal micropillars (1.0–8.3 μm edge length) machined via FIB at 30 kV; bulk polycrystals with grain sizes of 8, 70, and 340 μm. Test conditions: Micropillar compression at room temperature (strain rate 1 × 10⁻¹ s⁻¹); bulk polycrystal compression at room temperature and 77 K (strain rate 1 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹); TEM analysis at 200 kV. Findings: Bulk room temperature CRSS is estimated at 33–43 MPa, approximately 10 times higher than that of pure nickel (~3.2 MPa).; CRSS follows an inverse power-law scaling with pillar size with an exponent of –0.63, independent of crystal orientation.; Stacking fault energy is determined to be 30 ± 5 mJ/m² based on Shockley partial separations of 3.5–4.5 nm (screw) and 5–8 nm (edge).; Yield stress at 77 K (260 MPa for 340 μm grain size) is slightly more than twice the yield stress at room temperature (127 MPa).; Dislocations are planar and smoothly curved with no preferred line orientation, indicating no significant anisotropy in edge and screw mobilities.; The shear-modulus-normalized CRSS of the HEA corresponds to a hypothetical binary alloy with 20–50 at.% solute concentration and ~4% atomic size misfit.; Young's and shear moduli are ~10% smaller than pure Ni, while the bulk modulus is 24% smaller than pure Ni.. Mechanism: The high CRSS is attributed to thermal solid-solution hardening driven by atomic size misfit (~4% between Cr and Co/Fe) rather than severe lattice distortion alone; the low stacking fault energy combined with a high shear modulus leads to wide partial separations that inhibit cross-slip, while the absence of orientation dependence suggests similar mobilities for edge and screw segments.. Limitations: The study notes that Goldschmidt radii may not provide accurate size misfit values, requiring ab initio calculations to estimate the true misfit of ~4.1%; the solid-solution hardening estimate is described as a rough order-of-magnitude calculation.. Future work: The authors state that full results of deformation experiments on bulk single crystals of the HEA will be published elsewhere and that additional studies are needed to improve understanding of factors like impurity contamination affecting CRSS.. Quote: "CRSS depends on pillar size with an inverse power-law scaling exponent of –0.63 independent of orientation."
